Show:

Further information:
DURBAN - KwaZulu-Natal health department head Sibongiseni Dhlomo has been issued with a notice to appear before the South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) over the “lack of meaningful progress” in dealing with the provincial oncology crisis.

In a statement issued on Friday evening, the commission said it had issued a “notice to compel KZN health MEC Dr Sibongiseni Dhlomo” to appear before it.

Dhlomo and his department were singled out in a damning SAHRC report released last year as having “violated the rights of oncology patients at the Addington and Inkosi Albert Luthuli central hospitals to have access to health care services as a result of their failure to apply with applicable norms and standards set out in legislation and policies”.

The report -- the result of a complaint laid by the Democratic Alliance in 2016 -- also found that the measures the provincial health department told the SAHRC it would put in place to end the crisis were “inadequate and unacceptable”.

The report came in the wake of revelations that Durban’s public oncology services had been stripped of practitioners, with doctors leaving for the private sector because of unsatisfactory working conditions that included a lack of working equipment.

“Ten months later and after exchanges of correspondence and meetings with the KZN provincial department of health, the commission remains concerned at the lack of meaningful progress. The commission has noted the numerous reports that many cancer patients still lack access to timely and appropriate oncology health care and that some may have already died,” the SAHRC said.

Dhlomo had been called to appear on 14 May in terms of the SAHRC Act. At the meeting, he would have to produce “certain information and documentation, as well as answer questions under oath that would be posed to him to enable the commission to decide on what action to take in order to positively impact on this undesirable situation”, it said.

Onco Oct Script 5 ( AM version at 8:52pm)

Nathi
“It wasn’t easy to lose one of your breasts, in my whole body there is nothing that I love more than my breasts.”

V/O
Nathi Molefe was diagnosed with breast cancer 5 years ago.

Nathi
“I don’t want to lie, but the first thing I thought was that I was going to die.”

V/O
She was treated at Helen Joseph and Charlotte Maxeke Hospitals in Johannesburg. After her mastectomy, she started a new job in KWAZULUNATAL, working with women who had breast cancer.

Link
“Cancer survivor Nathi Molefe moved to Durban to become a community educator for the Breast Health Foundation.

V/O
She’d heard how dire the situation was for cancer sufferers, but being on the ground brought it home. In June 2017, there were no oncologists and radiotherapy machines were in short supply.

Nathi
“Cause I worked there I have seen things going on in front of me. It made me sick because some of the ladies there, have died, still waiting for their treatment. Still waiting for the dates to come.”

V/O
It’s an issue that Health MEC Sibongiseni Dhlomo is well aware of. Carte Blanche has been following the story since 2015, when it became apparent that provincial patients were dying because the radiotherapy machines weren’t working. The MEC blamed a service provider.

Devi: those machines are able to treat 80 patients a day those machines are not working it means that 80 people don't have a chance at a healthy life. Why was it not picked up early and fixed?
MEC: well how do you know it wasn't pick up?
How do you know it was not pick up? It didn't pick up. That is why...
Devi: but nobody was fixing the machines
MEC: they were being fixed on and off
Devi: that wasn't good enough that's what I'm saying
MEC: In retrospect everybody says that
Devi: so at the moment who has the contract to maintain those machines
MEC: there's no contract

V/O
Last year the Human Rights Commission issued a damning report, with recommendations. Did anything improve? IT WOULD APPEAR NOT, AS THE KZN Health Department was summoned back to the HRC in May this year TO EXPLAIN.

Bongani Majola/SAHRC
“It is almost twelve month since this recommendation was made and the commission is not yet satisfied that all of them have been implemented and continues to receive reports that cancer patients, still do not have adequate access to the health care services they require.”

V/O
Sadly Nathi Molefe’s cancer returned and it has metastasized through her chest.

She tried to get an appointment to see an oncologist at Inkhosi Albert Luthuli Hospital, but was told to return in four months. She phoned her mentor Louise Turner at The Breast Health Foundation in Johannesburg.

Louise
“I said to her no, best thing to do now is we will bring you back to JHB. So she’s back here, started her treatment, 5/ 6 weeks ago, from chemo point of view. If she had stayed in KZN, she would not have started treatment yet.”

Link
When her cancer returned to save her life and get treatment she had to move back to JHB

Louise
I would be worried I would not move to KZN or let any of my family or staff stay in the province when it comes to cancer treatment.”

V/O
It pains Nathi and Louise to think of cancer sufferers in KZN. Like Zodwa, whom Carte Blanche featured earlier this year.

Zodwa
“I am scared when I see the people dying around me. When I see them die, I fear that I am going to follow them.”

V/O
Zodwa’s mother, Zanele, is worried. She sees death all around her.

Zanele
“If I am not mistaken, 5 people have died since she’s been there.”

V/O
Zodwa was diagnosed in 2017, but couldn’t get treatment because of the lack of oncologists.

“They haven’t told us anything about when they are going to start the chemo. They said that they don’t deal with cancer – Albert Luthuli does, which means that they are a waiting room.”

Link (Revoice whole link - change cervIcal to cervical…emphasis on cal)

In February we met Zodwa at Prince Mshiyeni hospital and she had stage 4 cervical cancer and was still waiting for cancer treatment.

Claire
“I can’t imagine what it must be like to know you have cancer and to be told you have to wait to get your treatment?”

Opposition health spokesperson
“It’s devastating. And you people will tell you like the MEC or anyone else sitting in government, no we have all been touched, we musn't make politics about these issues. We are not making politics, we want you to be held accountable for what you are not doing. People are dying.”

V/O FIX SCRIPT
Dr Imran Keeka the OPPOSITION’S HEALTH spokesperson in KZN brought this lack of medical care to the attention of the Human Rights Commission in 2015. The oncology department has been in a state of collapse for a number of years and the patients are suffering.

Up Sound
“Are there any oncologists here today? We actually don’t know what’s going on.”

Zodwa
“Even then you don’t even get treated, they just keep giving you dates to come back – again and again.”

Claire
“Do you know how many lives have been lost due to the oncology crisis?”

Imran
‘We have on record 499 patients that we know of that have died. WE got this through parliamentary questions that were signed off by Dr Dhlomo, so he can’t deny it. That on it’s own is staggering.”

Link
Some things have changed since our last story in February this year, Addington Hospital has employed an oncologist

V/O
… and both radiotherapy machines are working.



V/O
Albert Luthuli now has oncologists and is operational. But the ISSUE REMAINS THE BACKLOG.

Dr Gumede
“The waiting period is 6 – 7 months”

V/O
There are also substantial waiting periods in the other cancer disciplines. (Changed from departments)

Link
The earlier the cancer is detected the better, if there are any delays in treatment, not only does the disease progress, but medical costs increase substantially and the chances of survival are slimmer.

V/O
Acting Head of KZN Health Dr Musa Gumede says they’ve spent R40 million and while they admit that there is a delay, there is movement.

Gumede
“We are not saying we have a Ferrari but we have a car that works.”

V/O
But will all the patients get the treatment they need on time?

Zodwa
“The doctors knew how sick I was and I still had to wait a long time.I was very upset to see people who weren't as sick as I was getting cancer treatment before me.

Link
“It’s hard to pinpoint the extent of the problem at the HRC hearing in May the acting HOD said there was a backlog of about 500 patients in Durban who had not been able to access cancer treatment. But in this report from the Department of Health, the backlog is estimated to be as much as 8000 patients in KZN.

V/O
THE KZN HEALTH DEPT WOULDN’T SPEAK TO US – OR RESPOND TO THE NUMBERS MENTIONED IN THE REPORT that was leaked IN SEPTEMBER– BUT REFERRED us to.
The National Department’s Dr Yogan Pillay. He is the author of the report which was written to make a case to Treasury for extra funds for oncology.

Dr Yogan Pillay - we need about R 1 billion to significantly improve in all provinces access to medical services specifically radiation oncology services.”


V/O
Dr Pillay says that the figure of 8000 as a backlog of patients was just an estimate.

Dr Yogan Pillay
“Working with the KZN Department of health we revised those numbers and in the meantime of course, the KZN Dept of Health has put some additional resources into their radiation oncology services, which has reduced the back log.”

V/O
But it’s not clear how an estimate of 8000 can be whittled down to as little as 556, with the addition of a few resources that have been brought back online.

Imran
“But I don’t trust those figures at all.”

Claire
“Because?”

Imran
“I had a complaint from a patient recently who said to me that they were told that they had received chemotherapy. But she says that she knows that she did not have chemo therapy because she did not go for chemotherapy. So who is to say that the system is not being cooked to make it appear better.”

V/O
DURING THE HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION INQUIRY, IT EMERGED THAT THE Department HAS a fuzzy approach to statistics. When asked what the waiting period was, after seeing an oncologist and starting radiotherapy treatment, Dr Gumede could not give the figures.

Up Sound
….eventually receive her first radiotherapy.

Gumede
“We would try and have to get those statistics in that format.

“Are you saying you don’t have the stat to say that how long does it take for those particular patients to receive radiotherapy? Isn't it?”

“Ja”

Louise
“The core values of the KZN Department of Health as trustworthy transparency, I am not so sure those values are being followed here.Are those stats right? Are they trying to play down the situation. Ho many patients have not come back that have been lost in that system, fallen through the cracks.


V/O
There are still many lives in the balance. The cautiously optimistic news is that Zodwa has just started chemo, BUT her prognosis is uncertain – THE treatment STARTED when her cancer was already at Stage 4.

The KZN Health Department assured the HRC that all backlogs would be cleared by the end of the year and the HRC has requested a closer working relationship with MEC Dr Dhlomo.

Nathi believes she had a lucky break.

“Do you think if I was still there in Durban, would I have survived?”




Promo 1 x 10 secs
KZN oncology is still in crisis. About 500 people have died from not being able to access cancer treatment. A LEAKED report estimates a backlog of thousands more patients in need of care.

Promo 2 x 15 sec
With a death toll of around 500 due to the oncology crisis in KZN, the Human Rights Commission called the Department of Health in to explain what, if any, progress has been made?
Imran: “We want you to be held accountable for what you are not doing. People are dying

Promo 3 x 15
“I just thought I was going to die.”
When Nathi Molefe heard she had secondary cancer, she left Durban and it’s oncology crisis to have treatment in Johannesburg. A leaked report reveals that the backlog of patients awaiting treatment in KZN is in the thousands.


Promo 4 x 30 secs

I am scared when I see people dying around me. When I see them die, I fear that I am going to follow them.

Zodwa who has stage 4 cancer has every reason to be scared. It is estimated that around 500 cancer patients have died in KZN because they have not been able to access adequate health care as promised in the Constitution. With a massive backlog how is the department going to find solutions to end this devastating catastrophe?

In a statement issued on Friday evening, the commission said it had issued a “notice to compel KZN health MEC Dr Sibongiseni Dhlomo” to appear before it. Dhlomo and his department were singled out in a damning SAHRC report released last year as having “violated the rights of oncology patients at the Addington and Inkosi Albert Luthuli central hospitals to have access to health care services as a result of their failure to apply with applicable norms and standards set out in legislation and policies”. The report -- the result of a complaint laid by the Democratic Alliance in 2016 -- also found that the measures the provincial health department told the SAHRC it would put in place to end the crisis were “inadequate and unacceptable”. The report came in the wake of revelations that Durban’s public oncology services had been stripped of practitioners, with doctors leaving for the private sector because of unsatisfactory working conditions that included a lack of working equipment. “Ten months later and after exchanges of correspondence and meetings with the KZN provincial department of health, the commission remains concerned at the lack of meaningful progress. The commission has noted the numerous reports that many cancer patients still lack access to timely and appropriate oncology health care and that some may have already died,” the SAHRC said. Dhlomo had been called to appear on 14 May in terms of the SAHRC Act. At the meeting, he would have to produce “certain information and documentation, as well as answer questions under oath that would be posed to him to enable the commission to decide on what action to take in order to positively impact on this undesirable situation”, it said.
